Keywords: atrial fibrillation
| catheter ablation | elderly | octogenarian | pulsed field ablation
ABSTRACT
Background: Pulse field ablation (PFA) is
an emerging catheter ablation
strategy
for patients
with
atrial fibrillation
(AF).



















Nonetheless, the safety and efficacy of PFA in elderly patients remains scarce. Hence, this study is to provide a comprehensive
review of PFA utilization in the elderly.
Methods: A systematic search was conducted from the inception of PubMed to July 2025 comparing the safety and efficacy of
PFA in elderly ( ≥ 75 years) and non-elderly patients. Safety outcomes were the rate of overall procedure-related complications,
major complications
(stroke/TIA, cardiac tamponade, phrenic
nerve injury, valve damage, myocardial infarction), and minor


complications. Efficacy outcomes include time to arrhythmia recurrence and rate of arrhythmia-free survival.
Results: Ten studies with a total of 5948 patients (900 elderly and 5048 non-elderly) were included in the analysis. In the elderly
group, the rate of overall and major complications was 3% (95% CI 2%–6%, I
2
= 0%) and 1% (95% CI 1%–2%, I
2
= 0), respectively.
However, elderly patients still had a higher risk of overall complications (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.29–2.91, I
2
= 0%, p = 0.020), major
complications (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.11–3.35, I
2
= 0%, p = 0.033), and minor complications (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.19–3.64, I
2
= 0%, p = 0.030),
compared to non-elderly patients. The rate of arrhythmia-free survival was similar in each group (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.41–1.59, I
2
= 0%,
p = 0.315). No significant differences were observed in procedural time (MD − 2.54 min, 95% CI − 14.76 to 9.68, I
2
= 88.6%, p = 0.595)
and fluoroscopy time (MD − 0.8 min, 95% CI − 3.11 to 1.51, I
2
= 80%, p = 0.392).
Conclusion: Our study demonstrated that, in the elderly, there was a similar efficacy in PFA for AF, but with a higher tendency
for complications, compared to non-elderly patients.
Abbreviations: AF, atrial fibrillation; AFEQT, atrial fibrillation effect on quality-of-life; AV, atrioventricular; AVB, atrioventricular block; PFA, pulsed field ablation; PNP, phrenic nerve palsy; PV,

pulmonary vein; PVI, pulmonary vein isolation; ROBINS-I, risk of bias in non-randomized studies of interventions.
Patavee Pajareya and Khamik Laohasurayotin are co-first authors.

Introduction


Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is a state-of-the-art strategy for rhythm
control in atrial fibrillation (AF). Its promising safety profile has
been demonstrated in real-world studies, showing reduced over-
all procedural complications through the use of electroporation, a
technique that selectively targets cardiac tissue while preserving
surrounding healthy
tissue 1, 2 ]. At 12 months post-ablation,
[










patients who underwent PFA showed improvements in AF Effect
on Quality-of-Life (AFEQT) scores, along with reductions in the
use of Class I/III antiarrhythmic drugs (AADs) and the need for
cardioversion compared with baseline [ 3 ]. However, the majority
of patients included in the landmark trials
of
PFA
were adults
aged < 75 years [ 4–8 ], and the efficacy and safety of PFA in elderly
patients ( ≥ 75 years) remain unclear.
Advanced age was a known risk factor for both short- and long-
term outcomes after catheter ablation, including periprocedural
complications, mortality, stroke, heart failure,
and
all-cause








hospitalization [ 9–11 ]. However, most patients in these previous
studies underwent
conventional thermal ablation [ 9–11 ]. More-

over, prior meta-analyses evaluating the efficacy and safety of PFA
did not specifically focus on the elderly population [ 12–16 ]. Thus,
the efficacy and safety of PFA in elderly patients (aged ≥ 75 years)
have not been determined.
Herein,
we conduct
a meta-analysis
to evaluate the safety and

efficacy of PFA in AF patients aged ≥ 75 years compared with a
younger population.
2 Methods


Our meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the







Preferred
Reporting Items
for
Systematic Reviews and
Meta-








Analyses
(PRISMA 2020) guidelines
and
was registered with







the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews






(PROSPERO; CRD No. 420251183868).
2.1
Search Strategy
Search was performed across three databases, consisting of MED-
LINE (via PubMed), EMBASE (via Scopus), and the Cochrane
Database
of Systematic Review
from
the
inception
of
PubMed




until July 2025. Two authors (P.P.
and K.L.) searched
indepen-



dently, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion with
the third author (W.T.). Search terms include “atrial fibrillation”,
“pulsed field ablation”, “elderly”, and “octogenarian” (Table S1) .

2.2
Eligibility Criteria
Our study included only adults aged 18 or older who were diag-
nosed with AF. All patients must have undergone PFA. Eligible
studies
must report outcomes of
PFA in
elderly AF
patients,











defined as individuals aged 75 years or older. Efficacy endpoints
include arrhythmia-free survival, procedural success, procedural
time,
and fluoroscopy
time.
Safety endpoints include
overall









complications, major complications
(including stroke, cardiac







tamponade, and
persistent phrenic
nerve
palsy
[PNP]),
minor








complications, and vascular complications. Only interventional
studies were selected with a restriction of the study design to only
randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled
trials (NRCTs), cohort studies, and case-control studies [ 17 ].
2.3
Outcome Definition

Efficacy endpoints include arrhythmia-free survival,
defined as

the patients who remain in sinus rhythm without recurrence of
atrial tachyarrhythmias (e.g., atrial tachycardia, atrial flutter, or
AF) at the end of the follow-up period. Procedural success was
defined as first pass isolation. Procedural time was defined as the
total duration from catheter access to catheter removal [ 18 ], and
fluoroscopy time was defined as the duration of fluoroscopy use
during the ablation procedure.
Safety endpoints were classified into major, minor, and vascular
complications according to the procedure-related complications
of previous literature on procedure-related
complications of








catheter ablation for AF [ 19, 20 ]. In general, major complications
are defined as any life-threatening events that result in permanent
end-organ injury, require
intervention, or
significantly
prolong

hospitalization, whereas minor complications are those that do
not
meet the criteria
for major complications [
20 ]. Vascular












complications
are defined as
complications
related to vascular



access
during the
ablation procedure.
All major, minor, and









vascular complications reported in each study were reclassified
to match the common criteria (Table S2) . Persistent PNP is









defined when the PNP-related symptoms last longer than
24
h

post-ablation [ 21 ].
2.4
Data Abstraction

Data
were extracted
for baseline
characteristics and outcomes.


Baseline characteristics included both patient
and procedural








characteristics. Patient characteristics comprised demographic




data, comorbidities, and use of AADs. Procedural characteristics
included ablation strategy (de novo or repeat ablation), ablation
target (pulmonary
vein
isolation [PVI]
or beyond
PVI),
and











mapping/ablation system. Categorical outcomes in both elderly
and non-elderly groups were collected as proportions of the total
population in each group. Differences
in categorical outcomes






between elderly
and
non-elderly
groups were reported as odds
ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For continuous
outcomes, data from both groups were extracted as mean with SD.
When studies reported only median with IQR, imputation meth-
ods were applied to convert values into mean and SD for analysis,
following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews [ 22 ].
Differences
in continuous
outcomes between
elderly
and
non-



elderly groups were expressed
as mean differences (MDs) with
95% CIs.
2.5
Quality Assessment

The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool was used to evaluate the
risk of bias in RCTs, while the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized
Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool was used to assess the
risk of bias in both NRCTs and Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS)

2.6
Statistical Analysis

All
analyses were conducted using
R
software,
version
4.5.0









(Vienna,
Austria). Because some outcomes were rare
(e.g.,








major procedural complications), studies with zero events in







both
arms (elderly and
non-elderly)
were excluded
from
the








head-to-head comparisons (i.e.,
OR and MD
calculations),
as







they provided
no comparative
value. Study-specific
estimates










were combined using generic inverse variance weighting under
a random-effects model,
assuming
inherent
differences across








studies. Heterogeneity was measured using Cochrane’s Q test and
the I
2
statistic. Between-study variance ( τ
2
) was estimated using
the Paule–Mandel approach for binary outcomes and restricted
maximum likelihood for continuous outcomes. Publication bias
was evaluated by visual inspection of funnel plot symmetry and
Egger’s test, with
a p
value
threshold of
0.10. Meta-regression








analyses were performed based on the percentage of paroxysmal
AF and the percentage of PVI alone to explore potential sources
of heterogeneity.
3
Results
Out of 2570 studies identified from all databases, 233 duplicates
were removed. The remaining 2337 records were screened by title
and abstract,
of which
170 articles
underwent
full-text review.







Finally, 10 studies [ 18, 23–31 ] (six NRCTs and four retrospective
cohorts), including 5948 AF patients (900 elderly and 5048 non-
elderly) who underwent PFA, were included in our meta-analysis
(PRISMA diagram; Figure 1 ).
3.1
Baseline Characteristics
Our study population was stratified
into the elderly and
non-








elderly groups. Among elderly
patients, the mean age was











79.1 ± 3.0 years, with 46% being female. Most patients presented
with paroxysmal AF (53%). The mean LVEF was 58.5 ± 6.6%,








and 47% underwent PFA limited to PVI alone. In the non-elderly
group,
the
mean
age was
64.1
± 7.0 years, with 32%
female.












Similarly,
the
majority
had paroxysmal AF (55%),
with
a
mean
LVEF of
58.7 ±
6.0% and
70% underwent PFA
for PVI alone.












A summary of baseline characteristics, including comorbidities
and details of the mapping and ablation systems used for PFA, is
provided in Table 1 .

I
2
= 0%, p = 0.033) (Figure 3B ).
Among
858
elderly
patients, 11
major complications
were








reported, including two strokes, one cardiac tamponade, one per-
manent pacemaker (PPM) implantation, one arteriovenous (AV)
fistula,
one groin
pseudoaneurysm,
one pneumonia,
and
four

documented among 4010 non-elderly patients. These comprised
15 cardiac tamponades, three strokes, three transient ischemic







attacks (TIA), three coronary artery spasms, three air embolisms,
one persistent phrenic nerve palsy (PNP), one hemoptysis, one
AV fistula, one pneumonia, and 15 unspecified events (Table S3) .

total of six studies 18, 26–30 ]
[

complication










rates. The incidence of minor complications in the elderly group

three studies
26, 29, 30
[

1.19–3.64; I
2

one vascular

complication, one
pericarditis,
one

segment
elevation,
one
transient
atrioventricular
block (AVB),

3.4 Meta-Regression Analysis

Meta-regression analyses
were conducted based
on
AF type







(paroxysmal vs. persistent AF) and the extent of PFA (PVI alone
vs. PVI plus ablation of non-PV substrates)
on arrhythmia-free

survival, procedural time, and fluoroscopy time. Neither AF type
nor the extent of PFA had a significant effect on arrhythmia-free
survival, procedural time, or fluoroscopy time, except for an effect
of paroxysmal AF on procedural time ( p = 0.026). Specifically, a
greater reduction in procedural time between elderly and non-
elderly groups was observed in studies with a lower proportion


of
paroxysmal
AF
(i.e., a higher proportion
of
persistent
or














permanent AF). The results of all meta-regression analyses are
presented in Table S6 . Bubble
plots illustrating the
correlation




between the percentage of paroxysmal AF and procedural time
are shown in Figure S4 .

2
= 0%) for overall com-
plications,
major complications,
minor
complications, vascular


complications, or procedural success. As a result, meta-regression
analyses were not conducted for these outcomes.
3.5
Publication Bias

All funnel plots appeared symmetrical (Figures S2 and S3 ), with
no
significant effects
observed in
Egger’s tests ( p > 0.10; Table

S7) .
Therefore, no
publication
bias was anticipated across all








comparisons.
4
Discussion


Compared with
non-elderly
patients,
AF ablation
in
elderly







patients was associated with: (1) a higher rate of overall, major,
and minor complications, while vascular complications remained
comparable; (2) no significant differences in the arrhythmia-free;
and (3) similar procedure and fluoroscopy times.
Although
the long-term efficacy of AF catheter
ablation
is








similar between elderly and non-elderly patients, the incidence
of
procedure-related complications
has
been reported to
be








significantly higher in elderly patients [ 32 ]. PFA is a novel non-
thermal ablation modality,
with
a lower complication
rate and



comparable efficacy compared to conventional thermal ablation
[ 1, 4, 33 ]. These notions further require a validation on the safety
and efficacy of PFA in
elderly populations, as presented in our
meta-analysis.
4.1
Efficacy Endpoints of PFA in the Elderly
In our study, no
significant difference
in arrhythmia-free
sur-











vival
was observed between elderly
and
younger patients.







Freedom from
arrhythmia recurrence in
octogenarians
was






71%, comparable to 77% in
non-elderly
patients,
consistent







with findings from
the EU-PORIA real-world outcomes study







[ 33 ] and prior studies on RFA and CBA in elderly popula-












tions [ 34–39 ]. Other procedural
efficacy outcomes were favor-








ably
comparable, with procedural
success
rates, procedural






times, and fluoroscopy times between the elderly and younger
counterparts.
Despite the
advancement
in
ablation
technologies,
the
in-







dept
understanding in
AF
mechanisms
has
been
barely
dif-










ferent, such that
the approach in ablation is unchanged. The











current
pragmatics remain
pulmonary
vein
isolation
and/or






additional lines ablation
which yet the
novel
PFA has been











applied
to the same
targets.
The
lack
of
long-term out-










comes
given the recency
of
PFA may argue as there remain










unknown
long-term rates of
lines
of block reconnection in








each ablated domain. However, with shorter procedural dura-







tion
and
higher
first pass isolation, the
utilization
of PFA









has rendered the more efficient workflow, minimized providers
and team staffs’ fatigue while retained
similar outcomes,
such




that the suitability of PFA
usage
in
elderly
should
be
highly











entertained.
4.2
Safety Endpoints of PFA in the Elderly
According to our
findings, it is
not
unexpected. The observed






outcomes can be explained by
the
increased
susceptibility
of











elderly individuals to post-procedural complications, which may
be attributed to progressive anatomical and physiological decline
with
aging, including alterations
in
the
immune system
and









impaired healing processes
[ 40–42 ]. Despite the seemingly less

favorable profiles,
the overall
complication
rate
remained low










(3%).
This observation is consistent with real-world data
for









patients undergoing PFA, supporting the favorable safety profile
of the procedure [ 33, 43–45 ].
Major complications
occurred in 1% of
elderly
patients, with









stroke being the most frequent event, as two cases were reported.
This likely reflects the elevated thrombotic risk in older patients
with multiple cardiovascular comorbidities, as represented by the
CHA
2
DS
2
-VASc score, the standard thromboembolic risk strat-
ification tool in current clinical practice guidelines [ 46 ]. Other
major complications in the elderly patients included cardiac tam-
ponade, permanent
pacemaker
implantation, atrioventricular






fistula, groin pseudoaneurysm, pneumonia, and four unspecified
events.
No post-procedural mortality was
reported,
suggesting






that PFA
may represent a
favorable
option for elderly patients





compared with
other
types of catheter
ablation,
which
have









previously been associated with a 3.2-fold higher risk according to
our prior meta-analysis [ 39 ]. Nevertheless, further network meta-
analyses comparing different ablation modalities are warranted
to provide
more precise and
comprehensive
evidence in this








population.
The
findings for
minor
complications
paralleled







those for major complications, as anticipated.
Importantly, no
cases of
persistent
phrenic
nerve
palsy
were









reported in the elderly,
with
only one
transient case observed.



This
likely reflects the
non-thermal
properties of PFA, which










minimize
collateral
injury
to adjacent structures. For vascular







complications, the results showed slight variation compared with
other safety endpoints, but no significant difference was observed
between elderly and younger patients. Contributing factors likely
include
sheath
size selection puncture
technique, and types of


vascular closures, with either devices, suturing or manual com-
pression, underscoring
the importance of operator experience







and procedural technique in minimizing complications. The use
of electroanatomical mapping systems has the potential to further
reduce procedural
complications
by
enhancing accuracy
and







enabling safer catheter navigation [ 47, 48 ]. However, only three
studies [ 24, 26, 30 ] in our analysis reported the use of mapping
systems, precluding meta-regression on this intervention. Further
studies are warranted to evaluate the impact of mapping systems
on procedural safety in PFA.
4.3
Clinical Implications
Our study provides important insights into the safety and efficacy
of PFA in elderly patients with AF. Although elderly individuals
demonstrated a higher
incidence of
complications
compared







with
younger
patients,
the absolute risks were
relatively
low,








with an overall
complication
rate of approximately 3% and
a











major complication rate of only 1%. These findings suggest that
Pacing and Clinical Electrophysiology, 2026
9 of 12



15148.0Page 10
while age is associated with increased vulnerability to procedural
events, the magnitude of risk remains modest in absolute terms.
Equally important,
procedural efficacy
did not
appear
to differ

by age. Arrhythmia-free survival, procedural success, procedural
duration, and fluoroscopy time were comparable between elderly
and younger patients. These findings underscore that advanced
age alone
does
not
compromise the effectiveness of PFA in










achieving durable rhythm control.
Taken together, these results support the use of PFA as a viable
therapeutic option
in
elderly
patients. However, clinicians







should be
aware that both
overall
and
major complication











rates were nearly doubled in this
population. This information

should be incorporated into shared decision-making discussions,
to
allowing patients make informed
choices about
treatment










after understanding the balance
between
procedural
risks
and




potential benefits.
4.4
Limitations
Our
study
had
several limitations.
First, many confounding










factors could contribute to the efficacy and safety of PFA,









especially
the types of AF
(paroxysmal
vs. persistent) and the









extent of
ablation procedure/techniques (PVI vs.
beyond
PVI).


To address
this, multiple meta-regression analyses were
made







to show
the effect of
these
factors on
both efficacy
and
safety










outcomes (Table S6) . Since the results showed that the percentage
of
paroxysmal AF affected the
procedural
time, this
outcome









should be interpreted with caution. Future studies in elderly AF
patients undergoing PFA would benefit from enrolling patients
with only
a
single
AF type (either paroxysmal
or persistent)












and
using a
single
ablation
strategy
(either
PVI
alone
or
PVI











plus ablation of non-PV substrates) to better clarify our findings.
Second, as no RCTs have specifically examined PFA outcome in
elderly patients
aged ≥ 75 years, all included studies
were
non-


randomized, which reduces the overall level of evidence. Thus,
well-designed RCTs regarding PFA in
elderly ≥ 75 years old are
recommended to confirm the efficacy and safety of PFA in elderly
AF population.
Third, only
a
limited
number
of
studies
were available for the


analyses comparing elderly and non-elderly groups with respect
to vascular complications
and procedural success, resulting in






wide confidence intervals for the pooled estimates. Accordingly,
these outcomes should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.
Fourth, the majority of included studies used pentaspine design
catheter, FARAPULSE PFA system. Therefore, the generalizabil-
ity could be limited. Lastly, residual heterogeneity may originate
from
incomplete reporting of
baseline
characteristics, which






limited the ability
to perform meta-regression
analyses.
Poten-

tial sources include
differences in patients’ comorbidities, PFA






ablation/mapping system, and follow-up duration. Nonetheless,
heterogeneity was low in most comparisons ( I
2
< 25%), suggesting
that the impact of residual heterogeneity was minimal.
5
Conclusion


In elderly AF patients, PFA offers similar rates of arrhythmia-free
survival
to younger individuals but
with
a
greater risk of
both



major and minor procedure-related complications.
